title: The Isdal Woman: Who Was the Traveller With Eight False Names?
subject: isdal
description:
Spy, smuggler, or a woman running from her past? What do you think she was hiding? 👇

On the 29th of November, 1970, a woman was found dead in Isdalen, a valley outside Bergen, Norway. Her suitcases held wigs, plain-glass spectacles and a coded travel log, and police found she had crossed Norway under at least seven false identities. This case file follows the investigation, the theories, and the tooth isotope and DNA work that has narrowed down where she came from, but not who she was.

Sources: NRK, "The Isdalen mystery" (2016); Mental Floss, "New Evidence Emerges in the Isdal Woman Case" (2017, on the University of Canberra isotope analysis); Discovery UK, "Who Was the Isdal Woman" (2022).

scenes.text: It was a Sunday, the 29th of November, 1970. A father and his two daughters were out walking in Isdalen, a steep, stony valley just outside the Norwegian city of Bergen.
In Norwegian, the name means Ice Valley. Among the boulders and bare birch trees, the older girl noticed something lying on the slope, and her father went to the police.
scenes.search: birch trees rocky slope grey sky

scenes.text: Officers found a woman. A fire had burned on the ground around her, and when a chemist tested the soil later, it contained traces of petrol.
She carried no wallet, no passport and no letters. Nothing on that slope told the police who she was, or where she came from.
Within a few weeks, detectives would learn that she had moved through Norway under at least seven different names, each one backed by a passport.
None of those names was real. More than fifty years later, Norwegian police still have a grave and a file, and no name for either.
Her body was taken to the Gades Institute, the forensic department in Bergen, and logged under a plain case number: 134/70.
scenes.search: old hospital corridor black and white

scenes.text: The examiners put her age somewhere between 25 and 40. She was about 164 centimetres tall, with brown eyes and dark hair.
Her teeth held the first real clue. She had around ten gold crowns, and a dental expert, Professor Gisle Bang, said work of that design was used in parts of southern and central Europe, and in Asia.
Inside her stomach were the remains of a large number of sleeping pills, a brand called Fenemal, many of them still undissolved.
The examiners concluded that she died from the effect of the pills together with carbon monoxide from the smoke. The burns, they wrote, may have contributed.
Tormod Bønes, a chemist from Kripos, the national criminal investigation service, confirmed that the soil where she lay contained petrol.
If she had taken her own life, she had done it in a very strange way, in a place that was hard to reach, with fuel she must have carried uphill herself.
Three days after the discovery, detectives checked the left luggage office at Bergen railway station. Two suitcases there had never been collected.
On a pair of sunglasses inside one of the cases, investigators found a fingerprint. It matched the woman from Isdalen.
The rest of the luggage looked like the kit of someone who did not want to be recognised. There were several wigs, and a pair of glasses with plain, unground lenses.
A tube of eczema cream had its label removed, so it could not be traced to a pharmacy or a doctor. On a comb and a hairbrush, the makers' marks had been rubbed off.
Clothes and toiletries were packed inside. Someone had gone through the cases item by item, taking away anything that could point to a country or a town.
There was also a writing pad. Its first page was filled with line after line of letters and numbers that looked like a code.
Among her belongings was one thing she had overlooked: a shopping bag printed with the name of a shoe shop in Stavanger, a city further down the west coast.
The writing pad took several days to crack. When it finally gave way, it did not hold a message for anyone. It held a timetable.
The letters stood for cities and the numbers for dates. Put in order, the entries traced a journey: Paris, then Stavanger, Bergen, Trondheim, back to Stavanger, and finally Bergen again.
In Stavanger, a shoe shop clerk named Rolf Rørtvedt remembered her. He had sold her a pair of blue rubber boots, the kind a person might wear for walking in wet hills.
At the Hotel St. Svithun, she had registered as Finella Lorck, from Belgium. The receptionist described a dark-haired woman with golden skin who spoke poor English.
In Bergen, she ate at the Hotel Neptun. A 21-year-old waitress there, Alvhild Rangnes, later put it simply: "I was impressed by her style."
Hotel registers in city after city showed the same habit. A new name each time: Claudia Tielt, Genevieve Lancier, Vera Schlosseneck, Alexia Zarna-Merchez, Elisabeth Leenhouwfr.
Police calculated that she must have used at least seven passports. Belgian investigators checked the identities she had claimed. Every one of them was false.
The log ended in Bergen, in late November. After that, the next certain record of her was the body found in Ice Valley.
One witness, though, told a different story. According to that account, she had not walked into the valley on her own that day.
According to that witness, a woman had been seen walking in Isdalen, pursued by two men. The two men have never been identified.
Little more than a week into the case, Bergen police brought in Norway's security services. In 1970, in the middle of the Cold War, false passports and a coded notebook meant only one thing to them.
The journalist Knut Haavik, who followed the case for decades, came to the same view. To him, she was a foreign agent.
Yet the official investigation pointed elsewhere. If someone had wanted to make her vanish, why leave two suitcases full of evidence at the main railway station?
And if she planned to die, why go to such lengths to erase her identity first, and then let a shoe shop bag survive?
No one came forward to claim her. On the 5th of February, 1971, she was buried in Møllendal cemetery in Bergen, in a zinc coffin, by a Catholic priest.
Sixteen policemen and two female police employees stood at the graveside. No family came. The grave was given no headstone.
Police closed the case as a suicide. The large dose of sleeping pills supports that verdict, and no suspect was ever named.
Against it stand the petrol, the fire and the long, deliberate removal of every clue. Critics of the verdict ask why a woman ending her life would need eight names.
The second answer is espionage. The wigs, the plain glasses, the coded log and the passports fit the picture, and so does the speed with which the security services became involved.
Some writers linked her to Israeli intelligence. According to Discovery, that idea is now seen as less likely, and no intelligence file proving any spy theory has ever been released.
The third answer is murder. Supporters point to the witness who saw two men in the valley, and to how the fire was set.
The problem is the lack of anything firmer. There was no identified killer, no motive anyone could prove, and nothing to connect the two men to her death.
Other explanations have been suggested over the years, from smuggling to a woman fleeing a dangerous past. Each one fits some of the facts, and none fits all of them.

scenes.text: For decades, the case stalled. What finally moved it was the part of her that had been kept: her jaw, preserved in a forensic archive.
In 2016, the Norwegian broadcaster NRK reopened the story with a long investigation of the case. New scientific tests followed within months.
Researchers from the University of Canberra analysed isotopes in her teeth, chemical traces left by the water and food of childhood.
Their results, reported in 2017, suggested she grew up in eastern or central Europe and moved west toward France in her teenage years. Some estimates place her birth around 1930.
A full DNA profile was also produced and published, in the hope that a relative somewhere in Europe might one day test their own DNA and find a match.
If that happens, it would answer the first question. It might not answer the others: why she came to Norway, what the journey was for, and who, if anyone, walked behind her up the valley.
Her grave in Møllendal still carries no name, and every name she used on her travels has turned out to belong to no one.
On that Sunday in Ice Valley, nothing on the slope told anyone who she was, and more than fifty years later, nothing in her file does either.
